questions.q: Why does an interpretability finding use claim, evidence, confidence, falsifier instead of the claim, method, result, limitation structure used for Projects 1-3?
options: Because interpretability write-ups don't need a claim at all
Because confidence and falsifier mean the same thing as method and result
Because the four-part structure is only for RLHF projects
Because an interpretability finding makes a causal claim about a mechanism, which needs an honesty check about what could have disproven it, rather than a reported training metric
questions.explain: A mechanistic causal claim calls for a structure built around how much to trust that causal story, including naming what would have falsified it — training write-ups report a metric and don't need that same check.

questions.q: What role does the falsifier section play in this write-up?
options: It is optional and can be skipped if the finding is strong
It names the specific result that would have disproven the claim, and states whether that result occurred
It restates the claim in different words
It lists unrelated future research ideas
questions.explain: The falsifier section states what experimental outcome would have broken the claim and whether it happened — a write-up without one reads as unfalsifiable, which is a red flag for a causal claim about internals.

questions.q: Why is a found circuit on SQL Pete described as 'suggestive, not a full explanation' of schema hallucination?
options: Because the patching experiments definitively proved the head's only function
Because SQL Pete has no attention heads
Because one component's causal effect on a handful of minimal pairs doesn't rule out other contributing components or other functions that same head performs
Because the finding was based purely on guesswork with no experiments run
questions.explain: Even a clean patching result for one head is one causal pathway, not proof that it's the only cause of hallucination or that copying column names is its only function — attention heads often serve more than one role.

questions.q: Why doesn't a circuit found in SQL Pete necessarily generalize to larger models?
options: Because activation patching only works on models smaller than 1B parameters
Because larger models never hallucinate schema names
Because larger models cannot be analyzed with activation patching at all

Because larger models have more capacity to spread, duplicate, or implement the same function differently, so a 1.5B-model finding says nothing directly about how a much larger model handles the equivalent behavior
questions.explain: The lesson is explicit that this finding is evidence about SQL Pete specifically, not a general claim about language models, since larger models can implement equivalent behavior with different, redundant, or more distributed mechanisms.

questions.q: What does this write-up feed into, and what does that mark for the lab?
options: Nothing; interpretability findings are not included in the final portfolio
A fifth new technical project in Chapter 6
A revision of Project 1's write-up only
Chapter 6 Lesson 25's portfolio assembly, as the fourth and last artifact — and this is also the last technical lesson in the research lab
questions.explain: This write-up becomes the fourth artifact (alongside Projects 1, 2, and 3) that Chapter 6's portfolio-assembly lesson slots in, and it closes out the lab's technical work before the course moves to presenting and wrapping up.
